title: IT Specialist: fix it, protect it, know what you own, write it down
intro: Support work is a method: ask what changed, check the cheap causes first, change one thing at a time, confirm with the person and document. These trackers let you practise that loop and the admin routines around it.
outcome: A worked ticket history, an inventory with warranty dates, one event log read, completed checklists and a storage forecast.

steps.title: Work a ticket properly
steps.what: A ticket is a short story: symptom, checks, fix, confirmation.
how: Open Helpdesk and log a Wi-Fi ticket. Tick the checklist items as you try them.
Add a note for each thing you change, then resolve it.
Open an urgent ticket and watch the SLA clock.
steps.done_when: A resolved ticket with a timeline someone else could follow.
mistakes: Closing without confirming with the person.
No notes on what was changed.
steps.ask: A user can't print: what do I check first?

steps.title: Know what you own
steps.what: You can't patch, insure or retire what you haven't listed.
how: Open Inventory and add every computer, phone and printer you manage.
Enter warranty end dates and read which are expiring.
Mark retired devices instead of deleting them.
steps.done_when: Every device is listed with an owner and a warranty date.
mistakes: Keeping the list in your head.
Deleting retired devices so there's no history.
steps.ask: Which fields matter most in an asset record?

steps.title: Read the event log
steps.what: The log shows the story: who signed in, from where, and what changed.
how: Open Event log reader and load the sample.
Read the failed-logon burst and the success after it.
Rank the findings and write what you would do first.
steps.done_when: You can explain the top finding and the evidence for it.
mistakes: Ignoring a success that follows many failures.
Clearing logs while investigating.
steps.ask: What does event 4625 followed by 4624 from the same address mean?

steps.title: Use checklists for routines
steps.what: Onboarding and offboarding are where access mistakes hide.
how: Open Checklists and run Onboard for an imaginary new hire.
Run Offboard for a leaver and note which step people forget.
Adapt one list to your own environment.
steps.done_when: Both lists run to the end and you've edited one for your world.
mistakes: Deleting a leaver's account on day one instead of disabling it.
steps.ask: What should happen first when someone leaves?

steps.title: Forecast and protect
steps.what: Disks fill and hardware fails on a schedule you can estimate.
how: Open Capacity and RAID and forecast a 1 TB disk at 70% used growing 25 GB a month.
Work out the downtime allowed at 99.9% availability.
Compare RAID 1, 5, 6 and 10 for four 4 TB disks.
steps.done_when: You can say when to order storage and why RAID is not a backup.
mistakes: Treating RAID as a backup.
Ordering storage when the disk is already full.

steps.title: Plan a vSphere build
steps.what: Work out hosts, networks and order of work before touching hardware.
how: Open IT tools > Virtualization (vSphere) and size hosts and storage for your VMs, with a spare host.
Enter your VLANs and subnets in the network checker and fix anything marked bad.
Follow the 10 steps in order, checking each one before the next, and save a Virtualization plan note.
steps.done_when: The network checker shows no bad items and every step has a check you can run.
mistakes: Two traffic types on one VLAN.
No DNS for the hosts and vCenter.
Counting snapshots as backups.
steps.ask: Size a small vSphere cluster for my VMs and check my VLANs.

steps.title: Choose tools on purpose
steps.what: Ten kinds of software cover most IT work; knowing which you have, and which you lack, comes before buying anything.
how: Open Software guide and mark each of the ten categories as have it, planned, gap or not needed.
Pick one gap, set the weights for what matters to you, and rank the tools.
Trial the top two or three on a few test machines, then write an IT tool decision note with the cost and your exit plan.
steps.done_when: Your stack is saved, and one gap has a decision note with a shortlist and a trial plan.
mistakes: Choosing by rating alone and skipping a trial.
Forgetting the exit plan and data export.
Treating a vendor-published ranking as neutral.
steps.ask: Which category should I cover first with a small budget?

steps.title: Study A+ Core 1: hardware, networking and troubleshooting
steps.what: Core 1 (220-1201) is 90 questions; troubleshooting and hardware carry over half the marks.
how: Open IT tools > CompTIA A+ and rate each Core 1 objective honestly from 0 to 3.
Work the port drill until you can say each service, port and TCP or UDP from memory.
Use the IP check, DHCP scope planner and mail records checker on a home network you own.
Take a 10-question practice quiz on your weakest domain, then read the reference for each miss.
Pick a symptom from the finder and say your theory, test and fix out loud, in the six-step method.
steps.done_when: Every Core 1 domain is rated, and your weakest one has a quiz score you can improve.
mistakes: Memorising answers instead of the reason behind them.
Skipping the hands-on objectives: open a spare PC, crimp a cable, pair a phone.
steps.ask: Which Core 1 domain should I study next and why?

steps.title: Study A+ Core 2: operating systems, security and procedures
steps.what: Core 2 (220-1202) is Windows, security, software troubleshooting and the professional habits of support work.
how: Open the Core 2 objectives and rate them.
Learn the Windows tools and commands, then run ipconfig /all, netstat -ano and sfc /scannow on your own PC.
Run the SOHO malware removal and change request checklists on an imaginary case.
Compare full, incremental and differential backups in the backup planner.
Paste a script into the script reviewer and say which lines you would not run.
steps.done_when: Every Core 2 domain is rated; you can name the 10 malware removal steps and the three change types.
mistakes: Treating Core 2 as memorisation of menu names: it is mostly choosing the safest next action.
Running a script you do not understand.
steps.ask: Walk me through the SOHO malware removal steps and why they come in that order.

steps.title: Learn the fundamentals: numbers, permissions and the command line
steps.what: Support work rests on a few basics: how computers count, how storage is sized, who may touch a file, and the same task in Windows and Linux.
how: Open IT tools > IT fundamentals and convert 87, 179 and 255 between decimal, binary and hex; check by adding the switched-on places.
Build a truth table for (A AND B) OR NOT C and say what each row means.
Enter a 1 TB drive in the storage calculator and explain why the PC shows about 931 GB.
Work out chmod 754, 640 and 1775 in the permission calculator and say who can do what.
Pick five tasks in the command finder and run the read-only commands on your own machine.
Open the Practice shell and finish all 11 tasks without opening the answers, then run a mixed Drill and practise the kind you scored lowest on.
steps.done_when: You can convert by hand, explain the missing drive space, read a permission string, finish the practice-shell tasks, and name the Windows and Linux command for a task.
mistakes: Setting 777 'to make it work'.
Running delete or format commands before testing on a throwaway folder.
Confusing kilobytes (1000) with kibibytes (1024).
steps.ask: Why does a 1 TB drive show 931 GB, and what does chmod 640 allow?

steps.title: Build your own toolbox
steps.what: A short list of safe, tested commands beats memory at 2 a.m.
how: Open Cheat sheets and read the PowerShell and Active Directory lists.
Try three read-only commands on your own machine.
Start a personal notes file of fixes that worked.
steps.done_when: A notes file with five fixes and the commands behind them.
mistakes: Pasting a command you don't understand into a production machine.
steps.ask: Which commands are safe to run first when a PC is slow?

steps.title: Predict which Group Policy wins
steps.what: Policies stack in order: Local, Site, Domain, then each OU from parent to child. The last one applied wins a conflict, unless a higher policy is Enforced.
how: Open IT tools > Infrastructure labs > Group Policy resolver and load the sample.
Before pressing Run, write down which value you expect for each setting and why.
Run it and compare. Read the 'overridden' list to see what lost.
Set Block Inheritance on the OU, then mark a domain policy Enforced, and predict again.
Change a link order and note that link order 1 wins inside one container.
steps.done_when: You can predict the winner for three settings, including one with Enforced and one with Block Inheritance, before running the tool.
mistakes: Forgetting Local policy applies first.
Thinking Block Inheritance stops Enforced policies: it does not.
Mixing up link order (1 is applied last, so it wins) with the order policies appear in a list.
steps.ask: Walk me through which GPO wins a conflicting setting for a computer in a child OU.

steps.title: Read and write LDAP data (LDIF and RBAC)
steps.what: A directory stores entries under distinguished names. LDIF is the text format for adding and changing them, and roles keep access manageable.
how: Open LDIF checker, load the sample, and read each problem it reports.
Fix the file until the verdict is clean.
Use the LDIF builder to make a user, then a group that lists that user as a member.
Open RBAC audit, load the sample and find the separation-of-duties conflict and the over-wide role.
Split the wide role into two and rerun.
steps.done_when: You can write a valid LDIF user entry by hand and explain why a role needs inheritance checks.
mistakes: Putting a plain-text password in an LDIF file.
Adding an entry before its parent OU exists.
Granting permissions to users directly instead of to roles.
steps.ask: What is the difference between ldapadd and ldapmodify, and what does a DN look like?

steps.title: Size a RAID, a backup scheme and a recovery plan
steps.what: RAID is not a backup. Large single-parity arrays fail during rebuild more often than people expect, and a backup you have never restored is a hope.
how: Open RAID rebuild risk and compare RAID 5 and RAID 6 for 8 disks of 16 TB.
Open Backup planner and compare full, incremental and differential for 500 GB with 5% daily change.
Note the restore chain length and the restore time for each.
Open Disaster recovery check, load the sample and fix the failing system on paper.
Run the DR checklist in Checklists.
steps.done_when: You can say why RAID 5 on big disks is risky, which backup scheme restores fastest, and what a tested restore looks like.
mistakes: Counting RAID as a backup.
Never testing a restore.
Keeping every copy in one place.
steps.ask: Explain RPO and RTO and how each shapes backup frequency and restore design.

steps.title: Triage a website and a load balancer
steps.what: Work from the bottom up: name, connection, secure handshake, then HTTP. A load balancer spreads load, but only a health check removes a dead server.
how: Open Website triage and walk a case: name resolves, TCP connects, TLS fails.
Look up 502, 503 and 504 in the HTTP status lookup and say which layer each points at.
Run the load balancer simulator with one server failed and compare the four algorithms.
Paste the sample access log and find the scanner probes.
steps.done_when: You can name the first layer to check for a 502, and explain why round robin is uneven when requests differ in length.
mistakes: Reading a 4xx as a server fault.
Assuming a load balancer is highly available by itself.
Treating a load balancer as a DDoS defence.
steps.ask: A user says the site is down. List your first four checks in order.

steps.title: Write tickets that get fixed first time
steps.what: A ticket is a message to someone who cannot see your screen. The first reply is usually a list of questions the ticket should already have answered.
how: Open IT tools > Ticket coach, load the vague example and read what a technician would still have to ask.
Rewrite it using the template until the score is Ready to work.
Check a closing note: write one with the cause, the fix, how you checked and how to prevent a repeat.
Use the priority tool on three cases and say whether you agree.
steps.done_when: You can write a ticket with who, what, when, what changed, the exact error, steps, what you tried, impact and environment, and a closing note someone else could reuse.
mistakes: Titles like 'help' or 'urgent'.
Closing a ticket with 'fixed' and nothing else.
Pasting a password into a ticket.
steps.ask: What nine things should a good support ticket contain?

steps.title: Take an incremental backup and prove you can restore it
steps.what: A backup only counts if you have restored from it. Use the practice area to take a backup, change files, take another (only the changes are stored), then run a restore drill to see how long recovery took and how much work would be lost. Damage a stored file on purpose and watch verification catch it.
how: Open IT tools > Backup lab, click Reset practice folder, then Take a backup.
Click Edit a file, Add a file and Delete a file, then Take a backup again. Read which files were added, changed and removed, and how many bytes were stored.
Click Drill on the first backup. What would you lose if you restored it today?
Click Restore and check the files. Why does it restore into a new folder?
Click Damage a stored file and Verify backup. Then try a restore of the affected snapshot.
Write the schedule you would use for a small office: what, how often, where, and who checks.
steps.done_when: You can state the recovery time and the data you would lose for your own setup, and you have a written check that a restore works.
mistakes: Calling a synced cloud folder a backup.
Keeping the only backup on the same disk as the originals.
Never testing a restore.
Backing up a database by copying its files while it is running.
steps.ask: Our backup job says 'success' every night. How do we know we can restore?

steps.title: Collect an inventory from real machines with an agent script
steps.what: A manual inventory goes stale. A small read-only script run on each computer reports the name, system, memory, disks and serial number, and the app imports the reports, matching by serial number first. Read the script before running it, and know exactly what it collects.
how: Open IT tools > Inventory and click Download the agent script. Open it in an editor and read what it collects. Note what it does not collect.
Run it on a computer you own: python inventory_agent.py --out pc01.json.
Paste the contents into Import from the inventory agent and import.
Run it again after a change (add disk space, rename) and import again. What was updated and what was left alone?
Write the note you would send to staff before running it on their computers.
steps.done_when: You have imported at least one real report and can list what the script collects and why you told the owner.
mistakes: Running an agent on computers you do not administer.
Collecting more than you need (files, app lists, user names).
Treating the serial number as unique when a vendor leaves it blank or 'To be filled by O.E.M.'.
Skipping the owner and warranty fields that only a person can fill in.
steps.ask: What should an inventory agent never collect, and why?
